newsitem.title: FRANCE: French civil service on strike over wages.
newsitem.headline: French civil service on strike over wages.

text.p: French civil servants went on strike over wage demands on Thursday, protesting against the government's refusal to make up for a salary freeze last year.
The call for a 24-hour stoppage made by seven trade unions is affecting some four million civil servants, from teachers to post office workers and street cleaners.
But the impact on the public was expected to be blunted as public transport workers, engaged in their own wage talks after staging their own strikes, were not involved.
Louis Viannet, head of the militant communist-led General Workers Confederation, told RMC radio in an early morning interview the strike was "an explosion of anger" over falling purchasing power.
But he cautiously added that it was too early to assess how the strike call would be heeded.

Demonstrations and rallies in major cities were expected to jam traffic. Many schools were expected to be closed and state hospitals and postal services to be disrupted as teachers, postal and hospital workers also complain about budget restraint and job cuts.
But automation of telephone and electricity services mean the stoppage will have little impact on consumers.
The stoppage by tax inspectors was one bright spot for taxpayers: the finance ministry has put off to next Monday from Thursday the deadline for sending in tax returns.

The centre-right government, eager to show its European Union partners and financial markets it will stick firmly to budget restraint to comply with criteria for the single European currency, has rejected union demands for a "catch-up" for last year's wage freeze.

"The government refuses to negotiate...although everyone admits there is a very serious problem with the purchasing power," Viannet said. "The government's stand towards civil servants encourages all bosses to tighten the screw on wages."
Unions have turned down the government offer of a 2.8 percent pay rise for 1997 and 1998 which they said will not compensate for a 1996 pay freeze.
They say wages are due to increase by one percent through 1996 and 1997 while prices are forecast to rise 3.6 percent.
The government disputes the figures, saying civil service wages will increase by 2.6 percent overall this year taking into account promotions.
